ἁπλουστέρᾳ οὔσῃ καὶ οὐδὲ ἀπὸ Μωυσέως εἶπε τι αὐτῇ συνιστῶν τὰ περὶ αὐτοῦ
ἀπείρῳ οὔσῃ γραφῆς, ἀλλ' ἐκ μόνης τῆς συνειδήσεως αὐτῆς μετέπεισεν αὐτήν. 136
{3Jο 4, 27}3Οὐδεὶς μέντοι εἶπεν· ᾔδεισαν γάρ, ὅτι πάντα ποιεῖ μετὰ κεκριμένης

ἐστὶν ἀτόπων μὴ δημοσιεύειν τὰ κοινωφελῆ. 141 {3Jο 4, 34}3Ὡς διδασκάλους τῆς

τοῦ θεοῦ. ὡς ἐπιθυμεῖ τις τροφῆς, οὕτω κἀγὼ τῆς σωτηρίας τῶν ἀνθρώπων. 142 {3Jο
4, 35}3Ὁ πνευματικὸς θερισμός, ὅ ἐστιν ἡ θεοσεβὴς ἐργασία, τὴν μὲν ἀπόθεσιν καὶ
τὸν ἀποθησαυρισμὸν ἐν οὐρανοῖς ἔχει, ἐν δὲ τῷ μέλλοντι αἰῶνι ἀπόλαυσιν
ἀτελεύτητον· οὗτος γάρ ἐστιν ὁ καιρὸς τῆς ἀνταποδόσεως. 143 {3Jο 4, 37}3Ὁ σπείρων
ἐστὶν ὁ Χριστὸς τὰ σωτηριώδη δόγματα κἂν διὰ προφητῶν εἰπών, θερισταὶ δὲ οἱ
ἀπόστολοι. 144 {3Jο 4, 37}3Οἱ προφῆταί εἰσιν οἱ σπείροντες, εἰ καὶ πολὺν ἔσχον
κόπον ὡς πρῶτοι τὰ τῆς εὐσεβείας σπέρματα ἐν ταῖς τῶν ἀνθρώπων ψυχαῖς
καταβαλλόμενοι· οἱ γὰρ μαθηταὶ οὐ τοσοῦτον ἔσχον κάματον ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν
πείθοντες τοὺς ἀνθρώπους. 145 {3Jο 4, 38}3Ὡς ἐμοῦ ὄντος τοῦ σπόρου κἂν διὰ
προφητῶν ἐλαλήθη πέμπω ὑμᾶς θερίσαι. οἱ μαθηταὶ καὶ τοὺς Ἕλληνας τῶν γηίνων
καὶ τοὺς Ἰουδαίους τῶν σαρκικῶν τοῦ νόμου λατρειῶν ἀποτέμνουσι καὶ εἰς τὴν ἅλω
ἀποτίθενται, ὅ ἐστι τὴν ἐκκλησίαν, ὅπου στάχυς τριβόμενος γίνεται σῖτος ὁ
ζωοποιῶν τοὺς πιστούς. 146 {3Jο 4, 40}3Σαμαρεῖται αἰτοῦσι τὸν Χριστὸν μεῖναι πρὸς
αὐτούς, οἵτινές εἰσιν ἀλλογενεῖς, καὶ οἱ συγγενεῖς αὐτοῦ τὸ κατὰ σάρκα Ἰουδαῖοι
ἐδίωκον αὐτὸν ὅτι «ἐχθροὶ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου οἱ οἰκειακοὶ αὐτοῦ» 147 {3Jο 4, 42}3Τὸ
οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ σωτὴρ ἀντὶ τοῦ ὁ Χριστὸς ὡς πᾶσαν μέλλων σώζειν τὴν οἰκουμένην
διηνεκῶς εἶπεν τοῦτο. 148 {3Jο 4, 43}3Οὐχ ὡς τιμῆς ἀντιποιούμενος ἐξῆλθεν, ἀλλὰ
τῶν πολιτῶν φειδόμενος· ὅτι γὰρ ἑώρων αὐτόν, ἐθυμοῦντο. ὃς ἐν τιμῇ ὢν τῇ θείᾳ
ἐσαρκώθη καὶ τὸν ἀτιμότατον ὑπέστη θάνατον διὰ τὴν ἡμῶν σωτηρίαν. 149 {3Jο 4,
44}3Ὧδε ἑαυτὸν καλεῖ τὸν προφήτην τὸν ὑπὸ Μωυσέως προανακηρυχθέντα, ὃς καὶ
προφήτης οἰκονομικῶς ἐκλήθη αὐτὸς ὢν ὁ τοῦ πνεύματος χορηγὸς ὡς θεός, δι' οὗ
προφῆται ἐπροφήτευον. 150 {3Jο 4, 48}3Σημεῖον τέρατος διαφέρει· τέρας γάρ ἐστι τὸ
παρὰ φύσιν γενόμενον, οἷον τὸ ἀνοῖξαι ὀφθαλμοὺς τυφλῶν καὶ ἐγεῖραι νεκρούς,
σημεῖον δὲ τὸ οὐκ ἔξω τῆς φύσεως ὂν οἷον τὸ ἰάσασθαι ἄρρωστον καὶ τὰ ὅμοια. 151
{3Jο 4, 50}3Πρὸ μιᾶς ἐπίστευσεν, ἐν δὲ τῇ ἑξῆς καὶ ἔργῳ ἤκουσεν, ὅτι γέγονεν ὃ

θεόν. 152 {3Jο 5, 2}3Προβατικὴ ἐκαλεῖτο, ὅτι ἐκεῖ συνήγετο τὰ πρόβατα τὰ μέλλοντα

προδιεγράφετο τὸ τοῦ βαπτίσματος μυστήριον, ἐν ᾧ πᾶν εἶδος ἁμαρ τημάτων

pass_a_gloss: She spoke from sense though as a Samaritan she did not know Christ. What he withheld from crafty Jewish questioners (I am he) he told the simpler woman, persuading her from conscience alone without Mosaic proofs she could not use. The disciples stayed silent because they knew he acts with care; they marveled at talk with a poor foreign woman and at his humility. Hiding common goods is absurd. He trains teachers of the world to put God's will above any meal; he hungers for human salvation as others for food. Spiritual harvest, that is godly labor, stores treasure in heaven and enjoys endless reward in the coming age. Christ sows saving teaching even through prophets; apostles reap. Prophets sowed first with heavy toil; disciples persuade more lightly from Scripture. His seed, though spoken by prophets, sends them to reap: they cut Greeks from earthly things and Jews from fleshly rites of the law into the church's floor where grain becomes wheat that gives life. Foreign Samaritans ask him to stay while Jews of his flesh kin chase him, as household foes. Savior means Christ who will save the world always. He left not for honor but to spare angry townsmen; the honored one took flesh and a shameful death for us. He is Moses' promised prophet, called prophet by economy yet as God the Spirit's giver. Wonders break nature (blind, dead); signs stay within nature (healing sick). Faith believed a day early and next day heard the deed; faith is strong with God finishing it. Sheep Gate held feast sheep for washing. Baptism's mystery was sketched there healing every sin; an angel's stir gave healing power at an unknown hour. We say
pass_b_english: understanding she said this; for being a Samaritan she did not know the Christ.

What he did not say to Jews who asked with guile—"I am he" (John 4:26)—he said to the woman, who was simpler; and he did not set before her anything from Moses to establish what concerned him, since she was unused to Scripture, but from her own conscience alone he persuaded her.

Yet no one said anything; for they knew that he does everything with measured understanding and reverence. They wondered that he spoke with a foreign and poor Samaritan woman, and they also wondered at his lack of pride.
It is among the most absurd things not to publish what benefits the common good.
As teachers of the inhabited world he teaches the disciples to prefer God's will to any food whatever. As one desires food, so I desire the salvation of human beings.
The spiritual harvest—that is, godly work—has its storing and treasure in heaven, and in the age to come unending enjoyment; for that is the time of repayment.

The sower is Christ, sowing saving doctrines even when speaking through prophets; the reapers are the apostles. The prophets are the sowers, even if they had much toil as the first to cast piety's seeds into human souls; for the disciples did not have so much labor when persuading people from the Scriptures.

As the seed being mine even if spoken through prophets, I send you to reap. The disciples cut Greeks away from earthly things and Jews from the fleshly worships of the law and set them on the threshing floor—that is, the church—where the ear, threshed, becomes wheat that gives life to the faithful.

Samaritans ask Christ to stay with them—they who are foreigners—while his kin according to the flesh, the Jews, persecuted him, because "a person's enemies are those of his own household" (Matthew 10:36).
"This is the Savior" (John 4:42) stands for the Christ, as one who is going to save the whole inhabited world; he said this continually.

He did not leave as one seeking honor, but sparing the citizens; for when they saw him they were angry. He who was in divine honor took flesh and underwent the most dishonorable death for our salvation.
Here he calls himself the prophet proclaimed beforehand by Moses, who was also called prophet by economy though he himself, as God, is the Spirit's supplier, through whom prophets prophesied.

A sign differs from a wonder: a wonder is what happens contrary to nature—opening blind eyes and raising the dead—while a sign is what is not outside nature, such as healing a sick person and the like.
The day before he believed, and on the next he also heard in deed that what he believed would happen had happened; for faith is strong when it has God as fellow-worker and perfecter.
It was called "Sheep Gate" because there the sheep to be slaughtered for the feast were gathered and their entrails were washed there.

Here the mystery of baptism was prefigured, in which every kind of sin was healed. An angel coming down into the water and stirring it put healing power into them. It is unclear on what day and hour the angel came down. We say
